mainTopic: Unclear divisions and gifts: half and half like רב יוסף, the silk, 'my sons,' and heirs who improve an undivided estate (בבא בתרא 143b)
overview: The גמרא finishes a challenge to רב יוסף, who holds that splitting something into two unspecified parts means half and half. It answers that the case of the מנחה brought in two vessels is special, because the person clearly wanted one big offering, and it rules like רב יוסף in three matters. Next come cases where a giver's words or intent are unclear. A man sends silk home, and the gift goes to sons, daughters, or a daughter-in-law depending on who it suits and who he most likely meant. A man who leaves 'my property to my sons' with one son and one daughter raises the question whether 'sons' can mean one son, and פסוקים are brought to show that it can. With a son and a grandson, רב חביבא and מר בר רב אשי argue whether a grandson counts as a 'son,' and a ברייתא about vows supports מר בר רב אשי. A new משנה then teaches that when older brothers or a widow improve an undivided estate, everyone shares the gain unless they first declared they were working for themselves. רבא limits this to growth that came from the estate itself, and the גמרא begins challenging him from רבי חנינא, a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא: fifty and fifty only works after the fact
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by saying that fifty-fifty is valid if already done. The גמרא learns from this that it should not be done from the outset, which seems to contradict רב יוסף's view that every such split is half and half.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he brought fifty in one vessel and fifty in the other, he has fulfilled his obligation. So 'if he brought,' yes, it works, but not from the outset. And if you think every case like this means half and half, then fifty-fifty should be allowed even from the outset!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last line of the ברייתא about the hundred-עשרון מנחה. It uses that line to challenge רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'if he brought' show the fifty-fifty split is only acceptable בדיעבד, after it was already done. If 'two parts' normally meant equal halves, as רב יוסף says, fifty-fifty would be the best way from the start. Since it is not, the challenge says an unspecified split is not automatically half and half.

keyTerms.meaning: From the outset, the ideal way to act
It would enter your mind, you might think
A tenth of an איפה, the standard measure of flour for a מנחה

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new ברייתא. It is the tail end of a ברייתא the גמרא started quoting just before this, and the inference from it continues a challenge already in progress.

phrases.english: And if he brought fifty [tenths] in one vessel
and fifty in one vessel, he has fulfilled his obligation.
"If he brought" means yes, it works,
but from the outset, no.
And if it should enter your mind

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא פַּלְגָא וּפַלְגָא הוּא,
phrases.english: that every case like this is half and half,
then it should be allowed even from the outset too!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ כׇּל כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא פַּלְגָא וּפַלְגָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge to רב יוסף that began before this section of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's view that an unspecified division into two parts means two equal halves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats fifty-fifty as acceptable only after the fact, so 'two vessels' does not automatically mean equal halves.

steps.title: The מנחה case is different: he wanted one big offering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. In the מנחה case, the person clearly wanted to bring as much as possible in one vessel. He only said 'two vessels' because one vessel cannot hold a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them?! There, it is obvious to us that this man intended a large offering from the start. He only said 'in two vessels' because he knew it is impossible to bring it all in one vessel. So we bring as much as we can in one vessel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge by showing the מנחה case has a special reason behind it. So it cannot be used against רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sixty-forty split comes from what this person obviously wanted: one offering as big as possible, so we fill one vessel to its sixty-עשרון limit. That reason does not exist in ordinary splits. In other cases, two parts can still mean half and half, as רב יוסף holds.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? The cases are not alike
We are witnesses, meaning it is obvious to everyone

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a person's obvious intention can override a default rule. This is why רב יוסף's half-and-half rule survives the challenge.

phrases.english: How can these be compared?!
There, we are witnesses
phrases.notes: An expression meaning 'it's obvious to all of us.'

phrases.english: that this man, from the start,
was intending a large offering,
and the reason he said "in two vessels"
is that he knew it is not possible
to bring it in one vessel;
so as much as it is possible to bring, we bring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 1 by distinguishing the מנחה case from ordinary divisions.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between the מנחה case and a general unspecified division.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The מנחה case has a clear intention for one maximal vessel, which ordinary divisions lack.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רב יוסף in three matters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules like רב יוסף against רבה in three disputes: dividing a field, the 'topic' question, and the 'half' question discussed here.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is like רב יוסף in three matters: field, topic, and half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a final ruling. In three disputes between רבה and רב יוסף, the הלכה follows רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'שדה' is the dispute about dividing a field between brothers. 'ענין' is whether certain actions are limited by the court's subject of discussion. 'מחצה' is our case: an unspecified division into two parts means equal halves.
steps.whatToRemember: The final הלכה: when someone divides something into two parts without saying how, it is split half and half, like רב יוסף. The מנחה case is an exception because of the person's clear intent.

phrases.english: And the halacha is in accordance with רב יוסף
in field, topic, and half.
phrases.notes: These are three separate disputes between רבה and רב יוסף. 'Half' is the one we were just discussing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב יוסף in step 2, the גמרא rules like him.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows רב יוסף: an unspecified split into two is half and half, and he is followed in the field and topic disputes too.

steps.title: Silk sent home: each piece goes to whoever it suits
steps.stepSummary: A man sent pieces of silk home without saying who they were for. רבי אמי rules that pieces fit for sons go to the sons, and pieces fit for daughters go to the daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who sent pieces of silk to his home. רבי אמי said: those fit for sons go to the sons, and those fit for daughters go to the daughters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a gift whose division was not spelled out. רבי אמי gives the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the father did not say who the silk was for, we judge by what each piece is suitable for. The type of fabric shows whether he meant it for his sons' clothing or his daughters'.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who sent
pieces of silk to his home.
רבי אמי said:
those suitable for sons go to the sons,
those suitable for daughters go to the daughters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about an unspecified gift after the ruling of step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Silk sent home without instructions is divided by suitability: sons' pieces to sons, daughters' pieces to daughters.

steps.title: If he has a daughter-in-law, the silk is for her
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רבי אמי's ruling: it applies only when the man has no daughter-in-law. If he has one, we assume he sent the silk for her.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when he has no daughter-in-law. But if he has a daughter-in-law, he sent it to his daughter-in-law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רבי אמי's ruling to a specific situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A father-in-law usually sends gifts like this to honor a daughter-in-law. So when there is one, his likely intention points to her, and the split between sons and daughters does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, introducing a limit on a ruling

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלֵית לֵיהּ כַּלָּתָא,
phrases.english: We said this only when he has no daughter-in-law,
but if he has a daughter-in-law,
he sent it to his daughter-in-law.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלֵית לֵיהּ כַּלָּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי אמי's ruling from step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the man has a daughter-in-law, the silk is presumed sent for her.

steps.title: Unmarried daughters come before the daughter-in-law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a further limit: if his daughters are not yet married, he would not skip them for his daughter-in-law, so the silk goes to the daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if his daughters are not married, he would not leave out his daughters and send it to his daughter-in-law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to the daughter-in-law rule of the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A father would not pass over his own unmarried daughters, who still depend on him, to give a gift to a daughter-in-law. So the presumption flips back to the daughters.
steps.whatToRemember: With unspecified gifts, we follow the giver's most likely intention: suitability first, a daughter-in-law if there is one, but never at the expense of unmarried daughters.

phrases.english: And if his daughters are not married,
he does not leave out his daughters
and send to his daughter-in-law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the daughter-in-law rule of step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If his daughters are unmarried, the silk goes to them and not to the daughter-in-law.

steps.title: Does 'my sons' mean one son, or does it include the daughter?
steps.stepSummary: A man left 'my property to my sons' but had only one son and one daughter. The גמרא asks what he meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said: 'My property goes to my sons.' He had one son and one daughter. Do people call a single son 'my sons'? If so, he meant to cut the daughter out, even from the tenth she usually gets. Or maybe people don't call one son 'my sons,' so he meant to include the daughter in the gift?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case and asks a question about word usage: what does 'my sons' mean when the man had only one son and one daughter?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to read it. If 'sons' can mean one son, everything goes to the son, and the daughter loses even her עישור נכסים, the tenth set aside for her dowry. If 'sons' needs more than one child, he must have been counting the daughter too, so she shares in the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: Do people call (how do people normally speak)
The tenth: the share of the father's property given to a daughter for her dowry

phrases.english: A certain man who said to them:
"My property to my sons."
He had a son and a daughter.
Do people call a single son "my sons"
and he came to remove the daughter even from the tenth;
phrases.notes: The 'tenth' is the part of the father's estate a daughter normally receives for her dowry.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, לָא קָרוּ אִינָשֵׁי לִבְרָא ״בְּנַיי״
phrases.english: or perhaps people do not call a single son "my sons"
and he came to draw the daughter into the gift?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about how the words of a gift or will are understood, following the earlier silk case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the plural 'my sons' can refer to a single son, which would exclude the daughter, or must include the daughter.

steps.title: אביי's proof: the sons of דן were only חושים
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a פסוק where one son is called 'sons.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear: "And the sons of Dan: Hushim."
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tries to answer the question with a פסוק. The תורה says 'the sons of דן' but names only one son, חושים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah itself uses 'sons' for a single son, then normal speech does the same. That would mean the man meant only his son, and the daughter is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, a phrase that introduces a proof

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:
"And the sons of Dan: Hushim."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That people call a single son 'sons.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 46:23: 'And the sons of Dan: Hushim.'

steps.title: רבא rejects the proof: חושים may describe many sons
steps.stepSummary: רבא says 'Hushim' might not be a name. It may mean Dan's sons were as many as bunches of reeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Perhaps it is like the school of חזקיה taught, that they were as many as the bunches of reeds!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on אביי's proof by reading the פסוק differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the school of חזקיה, 'חושים' is a description and not a name: דן had so many sons that they were like bunches of reeds. If so, 'sons' really means many sons, and the פסוק proves nothing about a single son.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Perhaps it is as the school of Ḥizkiyya taught:
that they were as numerous as bunches of reeds!
phrases.notes: He reads 'חושים' as a word meaning 'bunches,' not as a person's name.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא, דִּלְמָא כִּדְתָנָא דְּבֵי חִזְקִיָּה
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from 'the sons of Dan.' The idea that 'sons' can mean one son is not rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'חושים' may describe many sons and not be the name of one son.

steps.title: רבא's own proof: the sons of פלוא were אליאב
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a better פסוק where 'sons' clearly refers to one son.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: "And the sons of Pallu: Eliab."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא agrees with אביי's idea but gives a stronger פסוק. Here the single son has a clear name that cannot be read as 'many.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אליאב' is plainly one person's name, so the reading רבא used against אביי's proof does not work here. This shows that 'sons' is used for a single son.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, introducing a replacement for the rejected proof
Eliab, the only son listed for Pallu

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
"And the sons of Pallu: Eliab."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof rejected in step 9.
steps.raayaObject: That 'sons' can refer to a single son.
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 26:8: 'And the sons of Pallu: Eliab.'

steps.title: רב יוסף's proof: the sons of איתן were עזריה
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף brings another פסוק showing the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: "And the sons of Ethan: Azariah."
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives a different פסוק that makes the same point as רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again, 'sons' is followed by one clear name. Both proofs lead to the same answer: people do call a single son 'my sons.' So in our case the daughter is not included in the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: Azariah, the only son listed for Ethan

steps.whatToRemember: The proofs show that 'my sons' can mean a single son, so a man who left 'my property to my sons' with one son and one daughter gives everything to the son.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
"And the sons of Ethan: Azariah."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel proof to רבא's, from a different פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That 'sons' can refer to a single son.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א 2:8: 'And the sons of Ethan: Azariah.'

steps.title: Is a grandson called a 'son'?
steps.stepSummary: A new case: the man who said 'my property to my sons' had a son and a grandson.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said: 'My property to my sons.' He had a son and a grandson. Do people call a grandson a 'son,' or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second word-usage question. Does 'my sons' include a grandson?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a grandson counts as a 'son,' he shares the property with the son. If not, only the son receives it.

keyTerms.meaning: A grandson, literally 'son of a son'

phrases.english: A certain man who said to them:
"My property to my sons."
He had a son, and a son's son.

phrases.aramaic: קָרוּ אִינָשֵׁי לְבַר בְּרָא ״בְּרָא״, אוֹ לָא?
phrases.english: Do people call a grandson a "son," or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: קָרוּ אִינָשֵׁי לְבַר בְּרָא ״בְּרָא״, אוֹ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question to step 7, now about a grandson instead of a daughter.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the word 'sons' in a gift includes a grandson.

steps.title: Two opinions about whether a grandson is a 'son'
steps.stepSummary: רב חביבא says a grandson is called a son. מר בר רב אשי says he is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חביבא said: People call a grandson a 'son.' מר בר רב אשי said: People do not call a grandson a 'son.'
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give opposite answers to the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב חביבא, the grandson shares in the property. According to מר בר רב אשי, the word 'sons' means only the man's own children, so the grandson gets nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who holds that a grandson is called a son
An אמורא who holds that a grandson is not called a son

phrases.english: Rav Ḥaviva said:
People call a grandson a "son";
Mar bar Rav Ashi said:
People do not call a grandson a "son."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חֲבִיבָא אֲמַר: קָרוּ אִינָשֵׁי לְבַר בְּרָא ״בְּרָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the two opinions answering step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב חביבא: a grandson is included in 'sons.' מר בר רב אשי: he is not.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports מר בר רב אשי
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vowed not to benefit from a person's 'sons' may still benefit from that person's grandsons.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports מר בר רב אשי: Someone who is forbidden by a vow to benefit from 'sons' is allowed to benefit from grandsons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up מר בר רב אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the laws of vows (נדרים), we follow how people normally speak. Since a vow against 'sons' does not include grandsons, people do not call a grandson a 'son.' The same holds for a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא teaches in line with his opinion
One forbidden by a vow from receiving benefit

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא supports מר בר רב אשי: 'sons' does not include grandsons.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: It is taught in accordance with Mar bar Rav Ashi:
One prohibited by a vow from benefiting from sons
is permitted to benefit from sons' sons.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports one side of the dispute in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: מר בר רב אשי's view that a grandson is not called a 'son.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: one forbidden by vow from 'sons' may benefit from grandsons.

steps.title: New משנה: heirs or a widow who improve the estate
steps.stepSummary: If older brothers or a widow improve an estate, the gain is shared by everyone, unless they first declared they would work on their own share for themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A man died and left older and younger sons. If the older sons improved the property, the improvement goes to the middle, shared by all. If they said, 'Look at what our father left; we will work it and live off it,' they improved it for themselves. In the same way, if a widow improved the property, she improved it for the middle. If she said, 'Look at what my husband left me; I will work it and live off it,' she improved it for herself.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches who gets the profit when some heirs, or the widow, make the estate more valuable before it is divided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, work done on property that is not yet divided counts for everyone, so the gain is split among all the heirs. But if the workers announce at the start that they are working on their share for their own benefit, the gain is theirs alone. The widow follows the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: They improved, increased the value of
To the middle: shared by all the heirs
We work it and live off it, meaning we work on our own

steps.confusionAlert: Improving the property alone is not enough to keep the profit. What makes the difference is announcing beforehand that you are working for yourself.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If one left adult and minor sons,
and the adults enhanced the property,
they enhanced it to the middle.
phrases.notes: 'To the middle' means the gain goes into the shared pot for all the brothers.

phrases.english: If they said: "See what father left;
we are going to work it and profit from it,"
they enhanced it for themselves.
And similarly, a wife who enhanced the property
enhanced it to the middle.

phrases.aramaic: אִם אָמְרָה: ״רְאוּ מַה שֶּׁהִנִּיחַ לִי בַּעְלִי,
phrases.english: If she said: "See what my husband left me;
I am going to work it and profit from it,"
she enhanced it for herself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic: improvements made to an undivided estate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Improvements made by older heirs or a widow are shared by all, unless they first declared they were working their share for themselves.

steps.title: רבא limits the shared-gain rule to growth that came from the estate itself
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the משנה's rule that everyone shares the gain applies only when the property grew because of the property. If it grew because of the brothers' own effort or spending, the gain is theirs alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב חביבא, son of רב יוסף, son of רבא, said in the name of רבא: The משנה taught this only when the property grew because of the property. But if the property grew because of the brothers themselves, they improved it for themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the משנה about older brothers who improve the estate. רבא says the 'shared gain' rule is narrower than it looks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that if older brothers improve the estate, the gain goes to everyone. רבא splits this into two cases. If the estate grew from its own resources (the inheritance itself was used), everyone shares. If it grew because the brothers put in their own effort or spending, they keep the gain.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only... (a formula that limits a rule to a specific case)
They improved it for themselves, so the gain is theirs

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two phrases. 'מחמת נכסים' means the growth came from the estate itself, so it is shared. 'מחמת עצמן' means it came from the brothers' own work or money, so it is theirs.
steps.whyThisMatters: This distinction decides who owns the profit whenever some heirs work on property that has not yet been divided.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חֲבִיבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יוֹסֵף
phrases.english: Rav Chaviva, son of Rav Yosef, said
son of Rava, in the name of Rava:
They taught this only
where the property grew because of the property,
but if the property grew because of themselves,
phrases.notes: Because of the brothers' own effort or own spending.

phrases.english: they improved it for themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חֲבִיבָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא, מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the משנה's rule (Step 15) that gains made by older brothers or a widow are shared by all.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Gain is shared only when the property grew from the estate's own resources. Gain produced by the brothers' own effort or spending belongs to them.

steps.title: A challenge to רבא from a statement of רבי חנינא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks 'Is that so?' and begins quoting רבי חנינא, who speaks about a case where the father left his sons almost nothing. The quote continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי חנינא said: Even if their father left them nothing but...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's distinction. It is starting to quote רבי חנינא, and the rest of his statement comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אִינִי' signals that the גמרא doubts what was just said. The word 'אפילו' (even) suggests רבי חנינא will describe an extreme case where the father left almost nothing, and the brothers did most of the work. Such a case seems to clash with רבא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [so-and-so] say...? (brings a source that contradicts)
An אמורא whose statement is used to challenge רבא
He did not leave them (as inheritance)

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't Rabbi Chanina say:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא הִנִּיחַ לָהֶם אֲבִיהֶם אֶלָּא
phrases.english: Even if their father left them nothing but

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's distinction from Step 16 using a statement of רבי חנינא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that gains made through the brothers' own effort or spending belong only to them.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא's statement begins with 'even if the father left them almost nothing.' This points to a case where the gain came mostly from the brothers, yet it seems to be treated as shared. The full statement continues on the next amud.
